  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The dataset contains 76,655 trials across 8 mice after filtering for the five specified stimulation paradigms",
    "Combined stimulation paradigm accounts for the majority of trials (48,846 trials, 63.7% of filtered data), followed by ICMS Only (11,378 trials, 14.8%)",
    "Sham (3,505 trials), Dim Visual Only (9,603 trials), and Bright Visual Only (3,323 trials) are less represented, with Bright Visual Only having the fewest trials",
    "Overall success rate across all paradigms is 72.9% (SD=0.44), with mean Time-to-Target of 2.81 seconds (SD=2.08)",
    "Path Efficiency shows high variability (mean=0.47, SD=0.47, range 0.0009 to 29.82), suggesting heterogeneous task difficulty or behavioral strategies",
    "Average Speed is 12.50 cm/s (SD=4.46), while Angular Dispersion (AD) averages 0.38 (SD=0.24, max=1.0)"
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "Sample size imbalance is extreme: Combined has 14.7× more trials than Bright Visual Only and 13.9× more than Sham, limiting statistical power for between-paradigm comparisons",
    "The large standard deviations relative to means for Path Efficiency (SD/mean ≈ 0.98) and Time-to-Target (SD/mean ≈ 0.74) indicate substantial within-paradigm variability that may obscure between-group effects",
    "Success rate variability (SD=0.44) near the overall mean (0.73) suggests some paradigms may cluster near ceiling/floor effects, but paradigm-specific rates cannot be determined from aggregate data alone",
    "The maximum Path Efficiency value (29.82) is extreme relative to the theoretical maximum of 1.0, indicating possible data quality issues or calculation anomalies that may differentially affect certain paradigms"
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "The dataset is heavily dominated by Combined stimulation trials, which constrains confident inference about relative performance across paradigms. The high variability in Path Efficiency and presence of extreme outliers suggests that navigation strategies differ substantially across trials, possibly reflecting paradigm-specific effects on exploratory behavior. Without paradigm-specific means and standard deviations, claims about which stimulation condition optimizes navigation performance are uncertain. The near-ceiling overall success rate (73%) combined with high Time-to-Target variance suggests a speed-accuracy tradeoff that may manifest differently across stimulation types.",
  "limitations": [
    "No paradigm-specific descriptive statistics are provided in the artifacts—only global summaries across all paradigms",
    "Severe sample size imbalance (Combined >> others) prevents reliable between-paradigm comparisons without appropriate weighting or resampling",
    "The extreme Path Efficiency maximum (29.82) exceeds the theoretical bound of 1.0, indicating potential data quality issues or definitional inconsistencies",
    "Single replication (Run 1) with temperature 0.25 and summary-only data view may limit generalizability",
    "No information about trial structure, learning effects, or temporal dynamics within sessions",
    "Mouse identity is available but not analyzed—potential clustering by subject is unaddressed",
    "The 'summary_only' data view may have aggregated or transformed raw measurements in ways that obscure paradigm-specific patterns"
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Request paradigm-stratified descriptive statistics (means, SDs, n per paradigm) and visualizations (boxplots or violin plots) for all five response variables to enable direct comparison. Conduct formal statistical testing (ANOVA or mixed-effects models with Mouse as random effect) accounting for sample size imbalance. Examine the Path Efficiency distribution for outliers and verify calculation methodology. If feasible, obtain trial-level data to assess learning curves and temporal dependencies within each paradigm."
}
